RESULTS 123

To interrogate early mucosal immune dynamics, we conducted a case-control study of 16 124

participants aged 7 to 57 years old with incident SARS-CoV-2 infection, as well as 16 age-, sex-, 125

and COVID-19 vaccination-matched uninfected controls (Table S1). We optimized methods to 126

overcome technical challenges inherent to self-collected human upper respiratory specimens, then 127

quantified longitudinal viral loads and performed human exome-enriched RNA sequencing on 128

1,273 specimens from paired upper respiratory mucosal sites (oral cavity, nasal cavity, 129

oropharynx) collected daily or twice daily by each participant (Figure 1, Figure S1). Following 130

RNA extraction, RT-qPCR analysis of a human housekeeping gene, MYH9, revealed only minor 131

sampling variation over time within each participant (Figure S2A-C). Successful cDNA libraries 132

were generated from 99% of all self-collected upper respiratory human clinical specimens 133

attempted (1262 of 1273, Figure S2D). Despite high microbial background, human exome 134

enrichment enabled greater than 10 million human mapping reads in over 90% of samples 135

attempted (1165 of 1273, Figure S2E) with high reproducibility among technical replicates 136

(Figure S2F-H). Gene expression data exhibited anticipated biological patterns by participant sex 137

and anatomical sampling site (Figure S2I,J). From this unique dataset, we investigated the relative 138

timing and synchronization of IFN responses among upper respiratory sites within SARS-CoV-2 139

infected individuals, how early IFN responses relate to viral loads throughout infection, and the 140

impact of prior COVID-19 vaccination. 141

Early Type I IFN responses were synchronized across the upper respiratory mucosa of 143

individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2, and often preceded viral detection in the nasal cavity 144

Since SARS-CoV-2 can infect multiple anatomical sites within the human upper 145

respiratory mucosa,20 early mucosal immune responses at each site and their coordination can 146

influence the course of infection. Therefore, we first sought to investigate the relationship between 147

timing of viral presentation and IFN responses. 148

Robust and well-validated gene sets were available for Type I and Type II IFN responses, 149

but not for Type III IFN responses. Published Type III IFN gene sets (GO:003434221 and 150

M3946422) were small (<15 genes) and dominated by IFNL transcripts, which at the bulk tissue 151

level were lowly expressed, resulting in gene set module scores that poorly differentiated infected 152

from uninfected participants (Figure S3). 153

Within infected individuals, SARS-CoV-2 presents in the nasal cavity several days after 154

the oral cavity or oropharynx.18,19 Among infected participants, detection of SARS-CoV-2 in the 155

nasal cavity occurred at least one day later than the oral cavity or oropharynx for 88% of 156

participants (Figure S1), on average, 2.3 days later. Aggregated trajectories demonstrate this 157

delayed rise in nasal cavity viral loads relative to the oral cavity and oropharynx (Figure 1A). 158

Given these differences in the timing of viral detection among upper respiratory mucosal sites, we 159

asked whether IFN responses were also asynchronous and followed local viral detection. 160

To our surprise, we found that initiation of the Type I IFN response did not always follow 161

the presence of viral RNA within a site, but initiated concurrently in the oropharynx, oral and nasal 162

cavities shortly after SARS-CoV-2 detection in any site. Canonical Type I IFN-inducible genes 163

(e.g., STAT2, MX1, MX2, OAS1, OAS2, IFIT1) exhibited low and stable expression among 164

uninfected participants, but dynamic rises in all upper respiratory anatomical sites from individuals 165

DISCUSSION 410

Upper respiratory mucosal surfaces are the primary sites of respiratory viral infection, 411

replication and shedding, thus early immune responses that constrain viral replication at these sites 412

can reduce the risk of onward transmission. Using human gene expression measurements from a 413

unique set of paired samples from upper respiratory anatomical sites prospectively collected daily 414

by individuals who became infected with SARS-CoV-2, we characterized the timing and spatial 415

synchronization of early mucosal Type I and Type II IFN responses, their relative impacts on viral 416

replication, and their modulation by prior COVID-19 vaccination. 417

Despite differences in early viral load trajectories among the nasal cavity, oral cavity and 418

oropharynx of SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals, Type I IFN responses were initiated 419

concurrently and often preceded detectable viral RNA in the nasal cavity. This result supports that 420

testing for upregulation of nasal ISGs might enable earlier detection of viral infection to initiate 421

earlier treatment or infection control measures.32–35 Among unvaccinated participants with 422

sustained infection after SARS-CoV-2 challenge, ISGs were upregulated in the blood prior to the 423

nasal cavity, suggesting a potential systemic route for synchronization among upper respiratory 424

mucosal sites.15 425

Our analyses demonstrated that Type II IFN responses were not synchronized across upper 426

respiratory mucosal sites within infected individuals, but earlier initiation was associated with 427

lower local viral loads.  Moreover, earlier initiation of Type II IFN responses was observed among 428

participants with prior COVID-19 vaccination. Vaccinated individuals also exhibited subtle but 429

constitutively elevated expression of IFN-γ-inducible and TRM genes in the nasal cavity, which 430

were further upregulated shortly after viral infection. 431

Our results fortify the link between enrichment of upper respiratory TRMs, earlier initiation of 432

Type II IFN responses, and constraint of local viral replication in humans with naturally acquired 433

SARS-CoV-2 infection. TRMs have a recognized role in limiting viral replication,36–38 including by 434

rapidly producing IFN-γ upon SARS-CoV-2 exposure, as demonstrated  in ex vivo nasal mucosal 435

tissue39 and human lungs.25 In mice, airway CD4+ T cells recognizing SARS-CoV epitopes 436

induced rapid local IFN-γ production and reduced disease burden.40 In a trial of non-human 437

primates, IFN-γ induction by mucosal CD8+ T cells in the absence of SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing 438

antibodies (NAbs) yielded similar reductions in nasal viral load as Nab-inducing vaccines.41 In 439

human cross-sectional studies, higher magnitudes of a SARS-CoV-2-specific IFN-γ+ T cell 440

response in venous blood were associated with reduced risk of infection42 and the presence of IFN- 441

γ+ T cells in the upper airways was shown to prime viral recognition for enhanced viral clearance 442

and local control of SARS-CoV-2 replication.43 Longitudinal measurements from a SARS-CoV-2 443

human challenge study of unvaccinated individuals further support the role of T cells in local viral 444

clearance: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells infiltrated nasal mucosa within 1 day of inoculation for 9 445

participants with transient and abortive infections, but several days later among 7 participants with 446

sustained infection.15 Establishment of TRMs in the upper respiratory mucosa and early activation 447

of a Type II IFN response may constitute correlates of protection for vaccines intending to reduce 448

viral replication and forward transmission. 449

Several studies have demonstrated that intramuscular COVID-19 vaccination can elicit or 450

enhance early activation of TRM populations in upper respiratory mucosal sites,28,44–46 though 451

traditionally, intramuscular vaccines have not been very effective in establishing TRM in the 452

respiratory tract.28–30,40,47–49 Mucosal vaccines50 or hybrid strategies which follow intramuscular 453

vaccination with an intranasal adjuvant  (e.g. SARS-CoV-2 spike protein),51–55 have been shown 454

to substantially augment the establishment of TRMs in the upper respiratory tract.56 Pre-existing 455

cross-reactive TRMs may also contribute.57 Our study suggests that even low levels of TRM 456

responses generated by current COVID-19 vaccines can contribute to viral control, and the 457

potential of vaccine strategies to augment establishment of mucosal TRMs, prompt early viral 458

control, and block onward transmission. 459

Although earlier Type II IFN responses in both the nasal and oral cavities were associated 460

with reduced viral replication, enrichment of TRM signatures among vaccinated participants were 461

more evident in the nasal than the oral mucosa, suggesting anatomic differences in current vaccine- 462

induced mucosal immunity. We note that most studies assessing the establishment of TRMs in the 463

upper respiratory tract have focused on the nasal cavity or nasopharynx28,44,45 and most mucosal 464

vaccine candidates are administered only to the nasal cavity.58 Given that SARS-CoV-2 and other 465

respiratory viruses can initiate infection at multiple upper respiratory anatomical sites, even 466

complete protection of the nasal cavity may not prevent infection and transmission arising from 467

the oral cavity or oropharynx. Our results suggest that future vaccine candidates intending to block 468

breakthrough infection should have correlates of protection evaluated at multiple upper respiratory 469

sites (e.g. nasal cavity, oral cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx) where initial infection might occur. 470

This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting our findings. 471

First, analyses were based on a modest number of participants with sustained incident infection 472

(N=16), reflecting the logistical challenges of obtaining temporally dense, paired mucosal samples 473

beginning before the onset of infection in humans. Comparable temporal resolution has largely 474

been limited to controlled human challenge studies involving young, healthy, unvaccinated 475

individuals inoculated with early SARS-CoV-2 strains.15,33 While our cohort included 476

heterogeneity in age, vaccination status, health conditions, and viral variants, it was restricted to 477

however, daily mucosal immune profiling from multiple upper respiratory anatomical site starting 479

Second, because vaccination occurred later in our study period, vaccinated participants were 482

disproportionately infected with later SARS‑CoV‑2 variants, complicating efforts to disentangle 483

vaccine effects from variant-specific biology. All participants providing oropharyngeal samples 484

were vaccinated, precluding vaccine-related analyses for this site. Third, bulk RNA sequencing 485

does not resolve cell-type-specific expression, nor directly quantify protein abundance or 486

functional immune activity. While bulk mRNA sequencing captures tissue-level responses and cell 487

populations underrepresented in single-cell datasets (e.g., neutrophils),59 we do not measure 488

individual cells (including TRMs) or translated and secreted proteins, which are necessary to 489

directly attribute IFN production and antiviral activity to specific mucosal cell populations. 490

Functional profiling of upper respiratory resident T and B-cells would refine mucosal correlates 491

of protection induced by vaccination.60 Finally, gene-set-based module scores may differentially 492

reflect site-specific cellular composition, though our conclusions were robust across multiple 493

independent Type I and Type II IFN gene sets. 494

In summary, our study highlights the key temporal association between local TRM, early 495

induction of IFN-γ upon viral exposure, and delayed and reduced viral replication in the upper 496

respiratory mucosa of vaccinated individuals. 497

METHODS 498

Design of a COVID-19 Household Transmission Study to Identify Individuals with Incident 499

SARS-CoV-2 Infection, and Demographically Matched Uninfected Individuals 500

As previously described,61 between September 2020 and March 2022, individuals aged 6 501

and older residing in the Los Angeles area and sharing a household with a person recently 502

diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 were eligible to participate in our case-ascertained COVID-19 503

household transmission study (approved by the California Institute of Technology IRB, protocol 504

#20-1026). Participants completed demographics and health questionnaires, as well as daily or 505

twice-daily, paired, self-collected upper respiratory specimens (saliva and anterior nares swabs, 506

and for participants enrolled after November 2021, also oropharyngeal swabs) collected in 507

DNA/RNA Shield™ SafeCollect™ Swab Collection Kit  (Zymo Research Inc., Catalogue 508

#R1160-E) and Spectrum SDNA-1000 Collection Kit (Spectrum Solutions LLC, Draper, UT, 509

USA). These upper respiratory specimens underwent testing for SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA using 510

high analytical sensitivity RT-qPCR tests,18,19 with RT-ddPCR validation of viral load 511

quantification methods as previously described.18 512

Among 415 participants from 116 households, we observed 161 (38.8%) individuals with 513

laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, 82 of whom were considered secondary cases 514

within a household.61 Of these secondary cases, 16 participants were SARS-CoV-2-negative at 515

enrollment but subsequently developed sustained infection; these individuals were classified as 516

having naturally acquired incident SARS-CoV-2 infection, allowing longitudinal observation of 517

infection dynamics across multiple upper respiratory anatomical sites from the earliest days of 518

infection. From the 299 participants who did not develop SARS-CoV-2 infection, 16 uninfected 519

control individuals were selected, matched on age, sex, COVID-19 vaccination status, and 520

Generation and Pre-Processing of Human Gene Expression Data 524

In addition to longitudinal viral load quantification (previously described18,19), longitudinal 525

human gene expression was measured using an optimized and validated human mRNA sequencing 526

pipeline (described further in Supplemental Methods). Briefly, RNA was isolated using the 527

Quick-DNA/RNA™ HT kit (Zymo Research Corporation, Catalogue Number R2150) with a 528

DNase I digestion step to remove DNA. RNA was converted into cDNA using the lllumina RNA 529

Prep with Enrichment (L) Tagmentation kit (Illumina, Inc., Catalogue Number 20040537) and 530

cDNA libraries were subsequently enriched for human mRNA transcript sequences using the 531

Twist Bioscience for Illumina Exome 2.5 Panel. Resulting human exome-enriched cDNA libraries 532

were pooled and sequenced to a target depth of 25 million reads on a NovaSeq 6000 platform. 533

Samples which did not initially achieve quality control standards for RNA extraction and DNA 534

digestion, cDNA library generation, human sequence enrichment or sequencing depth underwent 535

modified protocols, described in Supplemental Methods. Samples not meeting quality control 536

standards following modified protocols were excluded from analysis. 537

Raw RNA sequencing data was mapped to human GRCh38.p1362 reference using STAR 538

v2.7.11b63 with default parameters, and pre- and post-mapping quality control assessment by 539

MultiQC v1.27.164 and Qualimap 2 v2.365 respectively. Raw gene counts were extracted using 540

featureCounts v2.22.1.66 Samples with fewer than 10 million human-mapping raw gene counts 541

were excluded from analysis due to insufficient coverage. Raw gene counts were then normalized 542

by specimen type group using the trimmed mean of M-values with singleton pairing67 implemented 543

Statistical Analyses 546

For longitudinal analyses, time was represented either as days relative to study enrollment 547

(for uninfected participants) or to the first detectable SARS-CoV-2 RNA in any anatomical site 548

within each infected participant. Longitudinal trajectories (viral load, individual genes, or module 549

scores) were summarized within stated time windows by pooling available sample-level 550

observations after rounding time to the nearest day, with 95% confidence intervals estimated for 551

each window by percentile bootstrap with 1000 resamples. Samples with no detectable virus (ND) 552

were imputed to a value of 1 copies/mL, and samples with detectable but not quantifiable viral 553

loads (NQ) were imputed to a value of 10 copies/mL. Cumulative viral load was calculated using 554

trapezoidal integration of linear-scale viral load measurements from a given participant and 555

anatomical site, then log10-transformed for downstream analyses. Trapezoidal integration was 556

also applied to linear-scale, normalized gene expression measurements to calculate cumulative 557

gene expression within given infection windows, then log1p-transformed for downstream analyses. 558

Module scores for pre-defined gene sets representing relevant immune programs (Type I, 559

II, and III IFN, and tissue-resident memory T cells) were computed from the log1p-transformed 560

normalized bulk RNA-seq expression matrix using a control-gene-subtracted approach: for each 561

sample, the mean expression of genes in the target set was calculated and compared with the mean 562

expression of a pooled expression-matched control background. For each target gene, up to 1,000 563

control genes were randomly sampled without replacement from genes with mean expression 564

within 90-110% of the mean expression of the target gene. The mean expression of the pooled 565

sampled control genes was then subtracted from the mean expression of the target gene set to yield 566

# COVID-19 study quantifying daily viral loads confirms throat samples are key to early diagnosis

**Authors:** Alexander Viloria Winnett; Natasha Shelby; Rustem F. Ismagilov

**Affiliations:** aDivision of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena CA, USA | bUCLA-Caltech Medical Scientist Training Program, Los Angeles CA, USA | cDivision of Biology and Biological Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena CA, USA

We appreciated the recent Letter by Todsen in Diagnostic Microbiology and Infectious Disease, highlighting the underappreciated role of the throat during early SARS-CoV-2 infection [1]. Unique longitudinal viral-load data from our COVID-19 household transmission study in Southern California strongly supports this point [2,3].

Between September 2020 and March 2022, 415 individuals from households where at least one member was recently diagnosed with COVID-19 were enrolled and collected daily nasal-swab, throat-swab, and saliva specimens for approximately 2 weeks. A subset of household contacts tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 at enrollment but later became infected (and continued daily specimen collection). Specimens from these individuals with incident infection provided an opportunity to quantify longitudinal viral loads in paired specimen types from the earliest stage of naturally acquired infection.

Quantitative, daily viral loads from paired specimens underscore the importance of the throat during early SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans. In 71 % (10 of 14) of individuals with incident infection, SARS-CoV-2 was detectable in the throat at least 1 day before the nose, with detection in the throat preceding the nose by a median of 2.5 days. Additionally, 64 % (9 of 14) of individuals reached high and presumably infectious viral loads in the throat before the nose [2]. Our data from naturally acquired infection of household contacts aligns with the SARS-CoV-2 human challenge study, in which infectious virions were detected in the throat at least 1 day before the nose for 67 % (12 of 18) of participants [4].

Testing the throat in addition to the nose increases clinical sensitivity during early infection. Using our quantitative viral load measurements, we predicted that COVID-19 antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag-RDTs) would exhibit up to 29.6 % higher clinical sensitivity during early infection when the throat and nose are tested, relative to testing the nose alone.[3] Two field evaluations including participants with early infections demonstrated similar (~20 %) increases in clinical sensitivity of the throat and nose with Ag-RDTs, compared to nose alone [5,6].

In contrast, two other field evaluations reported that throat and nose Ag-RDT was not superior to nose alone.[7,8] However, in one study, the high PCR positivity rate (83 %) among community members on the day of evaluation [7] suggests a population skewed towards later infection when the benefit of testing the throat is lower. In the other study,[8] clinical sensitivities were calculated against different references: nose-only Ag-RDTs were compared against nose-only PCR, while nose-throat Ag-RDTs were compared against nose-throat PCR. We have previously demonstrated that clinical sensitivity is overestimated when the nose alone is used as a reference, compared to both nose and throat [3].

We previously wrote a Correspondence in Clinical Infectious Diseases urging test manufacturers to validate their assays for use with throat swab specimens in the United States to enhance early detection [9]. We also encourage additional studies to observe early, longitudinal viral load dynamics in paired specimen types including throat swabs for other respiratory viral pathogens, such as influenza and RSV [10]. The throat appears to play an important role in early respiratory viral infection, and subsequently presents a unique opportunity for earlier detection of infection and more efficacious public-health and therapeutic interventions.

# Validating Combination Throat-Nasal Swab Specimens for COVID-19 Tests Would Improve Early Detection, Especially for the Most Vulnerable

**Authors:** Alexander Viloria Winnett; Timothy Stenzel; Rustem F Ismagilov

**Affiliations:** 1 Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA | 2 Division of Biology & Biological Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA | 3 California Institute of Technology Medical Scientist Training Program, University of California Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, USA | 4 Office of In Vitro Diagnostics, US Food and Drug Administration, Silver Spring, Maryland, USA | 5 Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA | 6 Division of Biology & Biological Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA

## Abstract

Early detection of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 infection by diagnostic tests can prompt actions to reduce transmission and improve treatment efficacy, especially for vulnerable groups such as immunocompromised individuals. Recent evidence suggests that sampling the throat in addition to the nose improves clinical sensitivity during early infection for both antigen and molecular coronavirus disease 2019 tests. We urge test manufacturers to validate tests for use with throat swab, in combination with nasal swabs.

Keywords: COVID-19, validation testing, early detection, rapid diagnostics, specimen types

Individuals with immunocompromise and other vulnerable groups at high risk for severe disease continue to rely heavily on coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) testing. This reliance often includes screening contacts before in-person interactions, to prevent the risk of exposure to individuals with presymptomatic or asymptomatic infections. Even in the absence of symptoms or known exposure, individuals with immunocompromise may also test themselves regularly to identify early infection and quickly initiate treatment. For this population—approximately 7 million people in the United States with primary immunodeficiencies or immunosuppressive treatment for cancer, transplants, or autoimmune disorders [1]—tests that detect early infection with high sensitivity are essential.

Among COVID-19 tests, the low cost, direct-to-consumer sale, and rapid results of at-home antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag-RDTs) make them an attractive and increasingly used diagnostic modality both for high-risk individuals and the general population [2, 3]. While the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has long been open to throat swab specimens for COVID-19 testing, all at-home Ag-RDTs are currently authorized only for use with self-collected nasal swab specimens [4]. However, nasal swab specimen Ag-RDTs have been demonstrated to have low to moderate (approximately 50%–80%) clinical sensitivity to detect infection in individuals, especially those who are asymptomatic and/or in the early stage of infection [5], when transmission of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) often occurs [6].

Several cross-sectional studies have demonstrated that Ag-RDTs exhibit higher clinical sensitivity when a combination of nasal (anterior nares) and throat (posterior oropharynx plus palatine tonsils) swabbing is used, compared with a nasal swab specimen alone (Figure 1A). A small study in Nova Scotia evaluated the use of combined nasal and throat swabbing for 2 separate Ag-RDTs (Panbio COVID-19 Ag Rapid Test Device and BTNX Rapid Response COVID-19 Antigen Rapid Test) in asymptomatic individuals [7]. Among 62 and 40 infected individuals respectively, 24% (Panbio) and 18% (BTNX) improvements in clinical sensitivity were observed by combining nasal and throat Ag-RDT results, compared with nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT results. This study also demonstrated a 13% increase in clinical sensitivity by testing a single combined throat-nasal swab specimen compared with nasal swab specimen alone in 38 infected individuals. A separate, large study of 827 infected individuals in Copenhagen, Denmark, recently demonstrated that combined nasal and throat Ag-RDT results improved clinical sensitivity by upward of 16% compared with nasal Ag-RDT results alone [8].

*Figure 1.: A, Summary of studies reporting the clinical sensitivity of combined throat-nasal swab specimen antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag-RDTs) compared with nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDTs. The difference between the clinical sensitivity of combined throat-nasal swab specimen Ag-RDT results and nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT results is shown in purple above each plot. Data are reproduced from cross-sectional field evaluations in Nova Scotia, Canada [7], Copenhagen, Denmark [8], and San Francisco, California [9]. These field evaluations had slight differences in design. “HCW collected” indicates specimen collection by a healthcare worker; “self-collected,” collection by the study participant. “Separate swabs” refers to designs in which test results represent the composite outcome of testing nasal and throat swabs separately; “combination swab,” designs in which the result was determined by directly testing a single swab used to sample both the nose and throat. Abbreviations: RT-PCR, reserve-transcription polymerase chain reaction. B, Conceptual schematic depicting the typical presentation of longitudinal severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) viral loads in nasal and throat swab specimens from the beginning of infection (first positive high-analytical-sensitivity test result in any specimen type), based on data from a study of individuals with naturally acquired infection in Los Angeles, California [10] and individuals inoculated with SARS-CoV-2 in London, United Kingdom [11]. The hypothetical nasal, throat, and combined throat-nasal Ag-RDT results are expected based on this typical presentation of viral loads, to illustrate why the increased clinical sensitivity of combined throat-nasal Ag-RDT over nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT would be greatest during early in infection and wane during later infection. Horizontal line indicates the limit of detection for Ag-RDTs. C, Clinical sensitivity of combined throat-nasal Ag-RDT (inferred from viral loads) and nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT results (participant reported) during different periods of infection, based on data from field evaluation of nasal swab specimen Ag-RDT with paired viral load quantification in Los Angeles [5]. Rightmost conditions (blue shading) in A and C highlight how cross-sectional evaluations that include time points late in infection may underestimate the benefit of combined throat-nasal Ag-RDT over nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT.*

Longitudinal viral load data suggest that infection stage influences the magnitude of the benefit of combined throat-nasal specimen Ag-RDT compared with nasal-specimen–only Ag-RDT. Daily viral loads quantified from prospectively collected nasal and throat swab specimens in individuals with incident SARS-CoV-2 infection revealed that the virus often presents in the throat days before presenting in the nose [10]. A simplified representation based on available data [10, 11] for the typical presentation of viral loads in the throat and the nose during early infection illustrates how the benefit of adding throat swab specimens to nasal specimen Ag-RDTs is expected to be greatest during the first few days of infection (Figure 1B). Indeed, based on quantitative viral load measurements in the throat and nose during the first 4 days of infection, Viloria Winnett et al [5] predicted that a combined throat-nasal specimen Ag-RDT would have approximately 25% greater clinical sensitivity than a nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT (Figure 1C). This prediction was similar to the benefits observed in the later studies performed in Nova Scotia, Canada [7], and Copenhagen [8]. In addition, supplemental data from Copenhagen shows that the benefit of combined throat-nasal Ag-RDT results over nasal-specimen-only results decreased with time from symptom onset among individuals from whom healthcare workers collected specimens, from 32% on the first day of symptoms to 13% thereafter [8].

The benefit of combined throat-nasal sampling extends to molecular COVID-19 tests as well. Among 14 individuals with naturally acquired incident SARS-CoV-2 infection, 10 (71%) had viral loads >1000 copies/mL in throat swab specimens for at least a day before viral loads in the nose rose to this level [10]. For many individuals, the delay was longer; more than a third of participants (5 of 14) had virus in the throat ≥3 days earlier than in the nose, and up to 7 days earlier for 1 individual [10].

In a separate study of individuals who underwent intranasal inoculation with SARS-CoV-2, 10 of 18 participants (55%) with sustained infection had detectable virus in the throat for ≥1 day before virus was detectable in the nose with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing [11]. Notably, replication-competent (infectious) virus was successfully cultured from throat swab specimens before nasal swab specimens in 12 of these 18 individuals (67%). These data suggest that if only nasal swab specimens are used, even molecular COVID-19 tests with high analytical sensitivity (including tests with low limits of detection; down to 1000 copies/mL) could yield false-negative results for individuals who may be capable of transmitting SARS-CoV-2 [12].

Analyses of paired viral load dynamics from the cohort with naturally acquired infection suggested that using combined throat-nasal swab specimens rather than nasal swab specimens alone with a high-analytical-sensitivity molecular COVID-19 tests would improve clinical sensitivity by >40% during the first days of SARS-CoV-2 infection [10]. However, because a subset of individuals may present with rising viral loads in the nose before the throat, combination throat-nasal swab tests are likely to yield higher clinical sensitivity than throat swab specimens alone. Indeed, the current Infectious Diseases Society of America Guidelines on the diagnosis of COVID-19 [13] recommend against the use of throat swab specimens alone for both molecular diagnostic tests [14] and Ag-RDTs [15].

Cross-sectional analyses of participant populations later in infection (after the first few days) are unlikely to observe the benefit of combining throat-nasal swabbing on Ag-RDT clinical sensitivity. For example, reanalyzing viral loads cross-sectionally between days 0 and 12 of infection in our group’s study [5] predicted only a marginal benefit (6%) for combined throat-nasal swab Ag-RDT over the observed clinical sensitivity of nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT (43%). This small, predicted benefit is similar to that observed in a later cross-sectional study of 96 infected individuals in San Francisco [9]. In that study, combined throat-nasal Ag-RDT increased clinical sensitivity from 54% (for nasal-specimen-only Ag-RDT) to 59% [9]. We note that the high PCR positivity rate (83%) among the 115 participants screened may suggest a study population skewed toward later infection. The clinical sensitivity of combined throat-nasal Ag-RDT may also be influenced by the throat swab specimen collection technique [16] or by whether a test designed for use with nasal swab specimens exhibits lower analytical sensitivity when used with throat swab specimens [13, 17].

Maximizing the clinical sensitivity of COVID-19 tests—both Ag-RDTs and molecular diagnostic tests—for early detection is paramount, particularly given surges in emerging variants with potential for evasion of humoral immunity [18]. To improve performance, Ag-RDTs and molecular COVID-19 tests need to be analytically and clinically validated by manufacturers for use with combination throat-nasal swab specimens, including clinical validation studies on (at least) symptomatic patient specimens. This combination throat-nasal swab test could use a single swab sampling both the throat and the nose or (to address consumer hesitancy) separately collected swab specimens from the nose and throat, which could be placed into the same elution medium.

Based on past FDA flexibilities offered for the validation of COVID-19 tests for emergency use authorizations (Supplementary Table), the FDA is likely to accept noninferiority studies, perhaps even only in symptomatic patients (historically, approximately 30 positive and 30 negative results are required for the emergency use authorization). For clearance, the FDA may accept evaluation of the combined throat-nasal swab specimen against a standard single swab specimen, showing at least in symptomatic patients that the combination specimen is not inferior (has equivalent or better sensitivity) in the requisite number of patients with positive results, usually 120 with positive and 500 with negative results for an over-the-counter test. The best way for developers to determine what the FDA expects is through the Q-Submission process [19], which is a no-charge FDA submission. The developers can ask their questions of the FDA and receive a response within 70 calendar days [19].

Although it may not be required for test validations, it would be particularly useful for studies to include populations for whom early detection has the most impact, such as the immunocompromised and those residing in congregate settings (eg, skilled nursing facilities and dormitories). These populations would demonstrate just how useful combination throat-nasal swab specimens are for populations at high risk of transmission or severe disease. We also suggest studies to investigate whether the use of combined throat-nasal swab specimens provide similar benefit for diagnostic testing of other upper respiratory viral infections, such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus.
